newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela says bombers face full might of S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says bombers face full might of S.Africa.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela on Monday vowed to use the full might of the government against bombers who launched a "dastardly" campaign of violence in South Africa.
Mandela's office said in a statement the bombers, whose attacks appeared to signal a white right-wing campaign of violence against Moslems, had no morality and lacked reason.
"There is no excuse whatsoever, in our democracy, for anyone to seek to pursue political aims by violent means...," the statement said after a weekend blast injured two at a mosque near Johannesburg.
"Those responsible will face the full might of South Africa's democratically elected and legitimate government."
A previously unknown extreme-right group has claimed responsibility for the attacks in the name of Christianity.

Mandela's statement said the blasts were "directed against all South Africans by a small group of people who know no morality, lack reason and do not seem to appreciate the full implications of their dastardly acts".
Acting police commissioner Zoli Lavisa appealed for calm.

"Any over-reaction, verbal or physical, could spark a new spiral of counter-violence which would play into the hands of the extremists responsible for these latest bomb outrages," he said in a statement.

Police minister Sydney Mufamadi, referring to right-winger who opposed South Africa's transition from racial oppression to democracy, said the bombers must be "racial bigots who have a propensity for the old order".

A telephone caller claiming to represent the previously unknown Boere Attack Troops (BAT) told state television the group was responsible for the weekend bombings near Johannesburg as well as two explosions near Cape Town on Christmas Eve.
Four people were killed and dozens injured by the two pipe bombs which exploded in the town of Worcester northeast of Cape Town on December 24.
The telephone caller said his group was opposed to Moslems and communists because they rejected Christianity.
The man claimed to recognise Mandela as president and accepted blacks as indigenous South Africans, but wanted, among other things, all Indians thrown out of parliament.
The Moslem Judicial Council and other Moslem representatives met at a Cape Town mosque on Monday for talks on the attacks.

State radio said the discussions included members of a controversial Moslem vigilante group -- People Against Gangsterism and Drugs (Pagad) -- which carried out fire-bomb and grenade attacks on the homes of alleged drug dealers.

Pagad gained prominence in August when supporters publicly shot and burned to death an alleged drug-baron, and since then members have clashed several times with police over their violent campaign against suspected criminals.
Police arrested two white mineworkers on Sunday after the three blasts in and around the conservative platinum mining town of Rustenburg in North West province.
The two later appeared in court where they were refused bail and ordered to appear again on January 10.
Explosives were allegedly found in the car they were driving and at one of the men's homes, a police spokeswoman said.
Mandela's office praised police for their work and promised that any culprits would be punished to the law's full extent.

Hardline right-wingers such as Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB) leader Eugene Terre Blanche issued frequent warnings of civil war ahead of the 1994 election, demanding self-rule for Afrikaners, but their potential to cause serious disruption had appeared to dissipate since the country's all-race polls.
Terre Blanche has said his group did not carry out the attacks, but "understood the degree of frustration" of right-wingers.
